draft.title: Acid dissociation constant
card: For a weak acid HA in water, HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻. The acid dissociation constant is Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻] ÷ [HA]. Water is left out of the expression.
Ka measures how far a weak acid ionises. A larger Ka means more ionisation at equilibrium, so the acid is stronger.
pKa = -log Ka. This turns very small Ka values into easier numbers, like pH does for [H⁺].
Because of the negative sign, a smaller pKa means a larger Ka. So a smaller pKa means a stronger acid.
draft.remember: Bigger Ka or smaller pKa means a stronger acid.

a.q: Which change shows that a weak acid is stronger than another weak acid?
opts: Its pKa is smaller
Its pKa is larger
Its Ka is smaller
Its concentration is higher
a.why: A smaller pKa means a larger Ka, so more of the acid ionises at equilibrium. A larger pKa is tempting because bigger numbers seem stronger, but the negative log reverses the order.
a.clue: The negative sign in pKa reverses the order of Ka.

b.q: Acid X has Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ and acid Y has Ka = 6.3 × 10⁻⁸, at the same temperature. Which statement is correct?
opts: X has the smaller pKa and is the stronger acid
X has the larger pKa and is the stronger acid
Y has the smaller pKa and is the stronger acid
Y has the larger pKa and is the stronger acid
b.why: X has the larger Ka, so it ionises more and is the stronger acid. A larger Ka gives a smaller pKa, so X has the smaller pKa. The option saying X has the larger pKa mixes up the direction of the negative log.
b.clue: Compare the powers of ten first, then flip for pKa.

b.best: X has the smaller pKa and is the stronger acid
